excerpts.author: jgm
excerpts.content:
Agree with the above, staker is a role (the entity that stakes funds) that is separate from the validator (the program that validates the chain through creation of blocks, and validates blocks through the creation of attestations).

Beacon node is probably safer than consensus node, as there will likely be consensus nodes in lower layers as well.  The name is already relatively well-known and no harm in keeping it when no alternative will be better.

Execution or application node for the current ETH1 node also seems reasonable, although possibly a little generic.  But something like "EVM node" is just ugly.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: We should not be naming things with a target audience of existing developers and users, we should be naming things with a target audience of future developers and users.  The "harm" in naming things poorly is that it creates confusion for new developers and new users.  The goal with naming should be that someone new to the ecosystem can fairly quickly ramp up and get an intuitive idea for how the system works without needing to go rewrite their internal language=>concept mapping.

excerpts.author: jgm
excerpts.content: Sure, but we should also try to name things such that they won't lead to confusion, either immediately or one or two (or however far we can see) updates down the line.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: While validators do validate blocks, that isn't what differentiates them from anyone else.  *Everyone* validates blocks, all light clients, "full nodes", and staking clients.  It would be like naming one of the 3 pieces "Ethereum Client".   All of them are Ethereum clients and giving a name like that leads to confusion rather than clarity, which is what we should strive for in naming.

excerpts.author: jgm
excerpts.content:
The argument against calling it a "staking node/client/peer/whatever" is that it isn't actually staking.  Staking happens elsewhere, by a different entity.  The piece of software actually carries out a number of tasks:
  - proposing blocks
  - attesting to already-existing blocks
  - (informing beacon nodes about required network subscriptions)
  - (handling sync committees, come Altair)

none of these things are staking in the sense in which it is generally known.

Of course, none of these things are officially validating either, but we do need a name for the thing that does the first two operations.

excerpts.content: And attestations are really the primary job of people running that client, producing blocks is almost like a side effect of that process.

(Although it is possible that this would happen at the beacon node level, in which case perhaps they will forever remain clients.)
